AP described several missing images, including one that showed a photograph of Donald Trump with Jeffrey Epstein, Melania Trump, and Ghislaine Maxwell inside a drawer. In a public statement, DOJ said that photographs and other materials would continue to be reviewed and redacted under the law as it received additional information. That statement gives a general review rationale, not a file-by-file explanation. The documented event is the disappearance of material from a public webpage after release. The report does not establish that DOJ destroyed originals, that records were permanently deleted, or that any oversight window was compressed. Those broader claims should be excluded unless supported by separate records.

proposal.description_long: On February 17, 1999, the Washington Post reported that Evercore Partners had agreed to acquire American Media Inc., the Florida-based publisher of the National Enquirer and Star. The reported transaction included Evercore assuming American Media’s debt. David Pecker, then chief executive of Hachette Filipacchi Magazines, was hired to become American Media’s chairman and chief executive. The distinction between buying the publisher and taking its top job matters: the transaction was led by Evercore, while Pecker became the executive responsible for running the company. The record’s earlier title incorrectly described Pecker as personally buying the National Enquirer and called the publication Mafia-owned. The cited 1999 acquisition report does not support either assertion. It also does not establish a Trump-related purpose or connection in the transaction itself. Pecker’s later relationship with Donald Trump should not be projected backward onto this corporate change. The revised description is limited to the ownership transaction and Pecker’s appointment, both reported at the time. Separate evidence would be required for the publication’s earlier financing history or for any later political relationship involving its leadership.

proposal.title: Reports Place Rybolovlev’s Jet Near Two 2016 Trump Campaign Stops
proposal.description_short: Flight-record reporting placed Rybolovlev’s jet near two Trump campaign stops in 2016; it does not establish that the men met or traveled together.
proposal.description_medium: A Philadelphia Inquirer report citing McClatchy flight records said Dmitry Rybolovlev’s aircraft landed in Las Vegas on October 30, 2016, when Trump held a rally there, and in Charlotte on November 3, near another campaign stop. The plane reached Charlotte less than an hour after Trump’s campaign aircraft. Rybolovlev’s representative denied contact. These movements do not prove the men met.
proposal.description_long: The Philadelphia Inquirer reported on flight records obtained by McClatchy that showed two airport overlaps between aircraft associated with Dmitry Rybolovlev and Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign. On October 30, Rybolovlev’s plane landed in Las Vegas on the day Trump campaigned there; the report said the jet spent about an hour and 20 minutes on the ground and taxied to a private hangar used by casino owner Sheldon Adelson. On November 3, Rybolovlev’s aircraft arrived at Charlotte Douglas International Airport less than an hour after Trump’s campaign plane, while Trump appeared at a rally in nearby Concord. Rybolovlev’s representative said the trip was for business and that he had no contact with Trump or his advisers. The reported records document aircraft movements and the representative’s denial. They do not establish that either man was aboard at the same time, that the two men met or communicated, or that the travel was coordinated. The original wording “cross paths” overstates what the evidence establishes; this draft keeps the claim at aircraft proximity.

proposal.title: White House Spanish-Language Website and X Profile Taken Offline in 2025
proposal.description_short: White House Spanish-Language Website and X Profile Taken Offline in 2025
proposal.description_medium: The Associated Press reported that the new administration took down the White House Spanish-language website within hours of Donald Trump’s January 20, 2025 inauguration; the Spanish-language X profile @LaCasaBlanca and a reproductive-freedom page were also disbanded. A White House spokesperson said the site was being edited and that archived content had gone dormant, and said the translation section would return. The evidence supports unavailability during the transition, not a permanent deletion claim.
proposal.description_long: Within hours of Donald Trump’s January 20, 2025 inauguration, the White House Spanish-language homepage became unavailable and showed an error page. The Associated Press reported the change the next day and identified @LaCasaBlanca, the White House’s Spanish-language X profile, and a government reproductive-freedom page as also disbanded. When asked about the changes, White House principal deputy press secretary Harrison Fields said the administration was developing and editing the website, that some archived content had gone dormant, and that it was committed to bringing the Spanish translation section back online. AP also noted that Trump had removed a Spanish White House page in 2017 and that the Biden administration restored it in 2021. These details distinguish the observed outage and account removals from an established permanent shutdown: the administration described the website status as transition work and promised restoration, though the report did not specify a date. The corrected entry should say the services went offline during the transition and include the administration’s stated explanation. It should not claim all Spanish-language government accounts were permanently deleted.
proposal.proposed_correction: Describe the pages as unavailable after the transition until reporting establishes whether the change was permanent, what accounts were affected, and whether Spanish-language content was restored.

proposal.title: Trump Publicly Opposed Approvals for Wind and Solar Projects

Bloomberg reported the statement and its context. The post is evidence of his stated position, while the supplied packet does not identify an implementing action or establish that all such approvals stopped.
proposal.description_long: On August 20, 2025, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the United States would not approve wind or solar projects, describing them as harmful to farmland and asserting that states relying on them faced higher electricity costs. Bloomberg reported the post as part of Trump’s public opposition to renewable energy and noted that it followed an Agriculture Department announcement ending support programs for clean energy on productive farmland. A public statement is evidence of the president’s stated position and can be reported as such. It does not, on its own, identify the agencies or permits covered, establish a blanket legal prohibition, or show that all wind and solar approvals stopped. The supplied packet contains no project list, implementing order, agency decision, or follow-up measurement of approvals. The revised title therefore describes the statement rather than presenting its broadest possible reading as a completed administrative ban. Any account of actual implementation should identify the governing directive and distinguish projects affected from those still under review. The statement’s cost assertion is also attributed to Trump; this record does not independently assess whether renewable projects increased electricity prices.

proposal.description_short: Trump’s Jan. 28, 2016 Iowa veterans fundraiser raised $5.6 million; $2.823 million went to his Foundation, according to the New York Attorney General’s filings.
proposal.description_medium: On January 28, 2016, Donald Trump held an Iowa fundraiser for veterans’ organizations rather than attend a televised Republican debate. New York Attorney General filings say the event raised about $5.6 million and that $2.823 million went to the Trump Foundation. The Attorney General later alleged that the Foundation’s handling of the funds constituted an improper campaign contribution. This fundraiser is separate from the $2 million damages order issued in 2019.
proposal.description_long: On January 28, 2016, Donald Trump held a nationally televised fundraiser in Iowa for veterans’ organizations while skipping a televised Republican debate. The New York Attorney General’s court filings say the event raised approximately $5.6 million and that $2.823 million of that amount was donated to the Trump Foundation, which was then expected to distribute the money to veterans’ groups. The Attorney General later alleged that the Foundation ceded control of the grants to Trump’s campaign, making the Foundation’s contribution an improper in-kind campaign contribution. That allegation and the eventual resolution belong to the later legal case; they should not be described as a finding that every fundraiser dollar was misused. In November 2019, a court separately ordered Trump to pay $2 million in damages to charities and imposed restrictions related to future charitable service. The stored January 28, 2016 date identifies the fundraiser, not that later court order. This draft aligns the title and descriptions with the dated fundraiser and clearly distinguishes the event from the judgment. The record should not combine the two dates or imply that the court order occurred in 2016.

proposal.title: Executive Order 13780 Revised Trump’s 2017 Travel Restrictions
proposal.description_short: Executive Order 13780 imposed temporary entry restrictions on nationals of six countries and paused refugee admissions in 2017.
proposal.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780 on March 6, 2017, revising his earlier travel restrictions. It imposed a 90-day entry suspension for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to exceptions, and separately paused refugee admissions. Iraq was removed from the covered-country list. Federal courts enjoined key provisions before or as the order was scheduled to take effect; those rulings came through separate cases and were later reviewed on appeal. The supplied Associated Press link is unrelated and does not support these details.
proposal.description_long: On March 6, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, “Protecting the Nation from Foreign Terrorist Entry into the United States,” replacing his January order. The revised order suspended entry for 90 days by nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to stated exceptions, and set a separate 120-day pause on refugee admissions. Iraq was no longer among the six countries. The order stated an effective time of March 16, 2017. Before that date, a federal district court in Hawaii temporarily blocked key provisions; a Maryland district court also enjoined parts of the order, and the government appealed. The Ninth Circuit’s opinion concerns the scope of the Hawaii injunction and should not be collapsed into the separate Maryland case. The order text and opinions are the relevant evidence for its provisions and litigation chronology. The AP URL attached to the original entry is a fact-check about Trump’s tweets and votes, not this order, so it cannot substantiate the existing description. This account describes the order and court challenges without treating the different injunctions as one ruling or suggesting the entire order was permanently invalidated at that stage.

proposal.title: Trump Pardons Former Border Patrol Agent Gary Mark Brugman
proposal.description_short: Trump pardoned Gary Mark Brugman, a former Border Patrol agent convicted of violating a detainee’s civil rights.
proposal.description_medium: The Justice Department’s clemency list records that Trump pardoned Gary Mark Brugman on December 23, 2020. It identifies a Western District of Texas conviction under the offense label “deprivation of rights under color of law,” with 27 months in prison and two years of supervised release. The Fifth Circuit’s opinion says Brugman punched and kicked a non-resisting detainee after the group complied with orders. The sources confirm the pardon and case facts, but not a documented motive for clemency.
proposal.description_long: The Justice Department’s official list of pardons granted by Donald Trump records a full pardon for Gary Mark Brugman on December 23, 2020. It identifies his case in the Western District of Texas, the offense as deprivation of rights under color of law, a sentence of 27 months’ imprisonment, and two years of supervised release. In United States v. Brugman, the Fifth Circuit affirmed his conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 242. The court’s account says that after a group of detainees complied with orders to sit on the ground, Brugman punched and kicked a man who was not resisting. The White House clemency statement emphasized Brugman’s military and Border Patrol service and listed supporters of his pardon request; that is the administration’s rationale, not a judicial finding about the underlying conduct. The available records establish the pardon, offense, sentence, and conduct described by the court. They do not establish a private motive for Trump’s decision or any connection between the pardon and a specific benefit.
